challenges.title: NumPy Arrays: The Foundation of Data Science
description: NumPy is the foundational Python library for numerical computing, used by virtually every data science and AI framework. Its core type is the ndarray — an N-dimensional array optimized for vectorized operations.

# NumPy basics import numpy as np arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) arr * 2 # [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] (vectorized!) arr.mean() # 3.0 arr.std() # standard deviation arr.sum() # 15 arr.reshape(5, 1) # column vector np.zeros((3, 3)) # 3x3 matrix of zeros np.linspace(0, 1, 5) # [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]
NumPy's power comes from vectorized operations — instead of looping over elements, you apply operations to the entire array at once, which is dramatically faster.
NumPy is the backbone of pandas, scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch. Understanding it is essential for AI/ML work.
Instructions
Implement a function arrayStats that takes an array of numbers and returns an object with four properties: sum, mean, min, and max (mirroring numpy's array statistics methods).
challengeSeed: // Simulate numpy array statistics in JavaScript
tests: var result = arrayStats([2, 4, 6, 8, 10]); assert(result.sum === 30, 'message: sum should equal 30 for [2,4,6,8,10].');
assert(result.min === 2 && result.max === 10, 'message: min should be 2 and max should be 10.');

challenges.title: Pandas DataFrames: Working with Tabular Data
description: Pandas is Python's primary library for data manipulation and analysis. Its core structure is the DataFrame — a 2D table with labeled rows and columns, similar to a spreadsheet or SQL table.

import pandas as pd df = pd.DataFrame({ 'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'], 'age': [25, 30, 35], 'salary': [70000, 85000, 95000] }) df['age'].mean() # 30.0 df[df['age'] > 25] # filter rows df.sort_values('salary') # sort df.groupby('dept').agg({'salary': 'mean'}) # group & aggregate
DataFrames are at the heart of data pipelines: loading CSVs, cleaning data, filtering records, joining tables, and preparing data for ML models.
The mental model maps directly to SQL: df[df['age'] > 25] is like SELECT * WHERE age > 25, and groupby().agg() is like GROUP BY ... HAVING.
Instructions

Implement a function filterAndAverage that takes an array of employee objects (each with name, age, salary), filters to only those with age >= minAge, and returns the average salary of the filtered group. Return 0 if no employees match.
challengeSeed: // 2. Return average salary of filtered employees
tests: var emps = [{name:'A',age:25,salary:70000},{name:'B',age:30,salary:85000},{name:'C',age:35,salary:95000}]; assert(filterAndAverage(emps, 30) === 90000, 'message: Average salary of employees aged 30+ should be 90000.');
assert(filterAndAverage(emps, 40) === 0, 'message: Should return 0 when no employees match the filter.');
assert(filterAndAverage(emps, 20) === 83333.33333333333 || Math.abs(filterAndAverage(emps, 20) - 83333.33) < 1, 'message: Should return the average of all employees when minAge is 20.');

challenges.title: Data Cleaning: Handling Missing Values
description: Real-world datasets are messy. One of the most common tasks in data analysis is handling missing values. In Pandas, missing values are represented as NaN (Not a Number).

import pandas as pd import numpy as np df = pd.DataFrame({'score': [85, np.nan, 92, np.nan, 78]}) df.isnull().sum() # count missing values df['score'].fillna(0) # replace NaN with 0 df['score'].fillna(df['score'].mean()) # fill with mean df.dropna() # remove rows with NaN

Choosing how to handle missing data is an important analytical decision: dropping rows is safe but loses data; imputing (filling) with mean/median is common for continuous values; using forward fill is common for time series.
In 2026, ML pipelines use sophisticated imputation strategies — including model-based imputation where a secondary model predicts the missing values.
Instructions

Write a function cleanData that takes an array of numbers (which may contain null or undefined values), and returns a new array where all null/undefined values are replaced with the mean of the non-null values. Round the mean to 2 decimal places.
challengeSeed: // 3. Return new array with nulls replaced by mean
tests: var result = cleanData([1, null, 3, null, 5]); assert(result[1] === 3 && result[3] === 3, 'message: Null values should be replaced with the mean (3) of [1, 3, 5].');
assert(result[0] === 1 && result[2] === 3 && result[4] === 5, 'message: Non-null values should remain unchanged.');
var r2 = cleanData([10, 20, null]); assert(r2[2] === 15, 'message: Mean of [10, 20] is 15, so null should become 15.');

challenges.title: GroupBy and Aggregation: Finding Patterns in Data
description: One of the most powerful data analysis operations is grouping data and computing aggregates within each group — exactly like SQL's GROUP BY.

import pandas as pd df = pd.DataFrame({ 'dept': ['Eng', 'Eng', 'HR', 'HR', 'Eng'], 'salary': [90000, 95000, 65000, 70000, 100000] }) # Group by department, get average salary df.groupby('dept')['salary'].mean() # dept # Eng 95000.0 # HR 67500.0
This pattern — group, then aggregate — is fundamental to exploratory data analysis (EDA). Common aggregations: mean(), sum(), count(), min(), max(), std().
In JavaScript, you implement groupBy using reduce() to build a grouped object, then compute statistics per group.
Instructions

Write a function groupByAvg that takes an array of objects and two strings: groupKey (the property to group by) and valueKey (the property to average). Return an object where each key is a group name and the value is the average of valueKey within that group.
challengeSeed: // 2. For each group, calculate mean of valueKey
tests: var data = [{dept:'Eng',salary:90000},{dept:'Eng',salary:95000},{dept:'HR',salary:65000},{dept:'HR',salary:70000}]; var result = groupByAvg(data, 'dept', 'salary'); assert(result['Eng'] === 92500, 'message: Average salary for Eng should be 92500.');
assert(result['HR'] === 67500, 'message: Average salary for HR should be 67500.');

challenges.title: Data Normalization and Feature Scaling
description: Before feeding data into machine learning models, you typically need to normalize or scale the features. This ensures no single feature dominates due to its scale.
Two common techniques:
# Min-Max Normalization: scales to [0, 1] normalized = (x - x.min()) / (x.max() - x.min()) # Z-score Standardization: mean=0, std=1 standardized = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
Example: If salary ranges from $30,000 to $150,000 and age from 20 to 65, a model without normalization would weight salary ~3,000x more than age just because of magnitude.
NumPy and scikit-learn provide MinMaxScaler and StandardScaler for this, but understanding the math behind them is essential.
Instructions

Write a function minMaxNormalize that takes an array of numbers and returns a new array where each value is scaled to the range [0, 1] using min-max normalization. If all values are identical, return an array of zeros.
challengeSeed: // Handle edge case where max === min
tests: var result = minMaxNormalize([0, 5, 10]); assert(result[0] === 0 && result[1] === 0.5 && result[2] === 1, 'message: [0, 5, 10] normalized should be [0, 0.5, 1].');
var r2 = minMaxNormalize([5, 5, 5]); assert(r2.every(function(x) { return x === 0; }), 'message: All-equal array should return all zeros.');
var r3 = minMaxNormalize([100, 200, 300, 400]); assert(r3[0] === 0 && r3[3] === 1, 'message: Min should map to 0 and max to 1.');
